tldr: The authors propose KINO, a hierarchical framework that bridges high-level semantic reasoning from Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and whole-body humanoid motion control via Reinforcement Learning (RL) using motion keyframes. By introducing a feature-based saliency sampling method that reliably guides the robot to target poses even with sparse keyframes, the system boosts task success rates from 44% to 92%.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of KINO. The VLM selects keyframes based on natural language instructions and scene images. A retargeting module adjusts target poses to match the object's size and position, and a lower-level reinforcement learning policy then generates joint-level whole-body torques and joint position commands.
overview:
Loco-manipulation—having humanoid robots transport objects in everyday human environments—is exceptionally challenging because the robot must coordinate delicate manipulation while maintaining walking balance. Recently, high-level reasoning with Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have gained massive attention. However, humanoids have high degrees of freedom and require millisecond-level dynamic balance control. Directly training VLAs for such platforms demands massive real-world data collection, making the approach difficult to scale. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (RL) policies can master robust whole-body motor control, but they struggle with multi-step, long-horizon task planning and semantic reasoning.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed KINO, an intuitive hierarchical architecture that places motion keyframes—target poses at critical task milestones—between a semantic VLM and physical RL control. The VLM selects the next keyframe from a predefined motion library. The framework then geometrically retargets this pose to match the object's current position and dimensions before passing it as a goal to the low-level policy. Furthermore, by introducing saliency-based keyframe sampling during policy training, the policy learns to hit crucial milestone poses accurately even when guided by sparse keyframe commands.

The authors validated their system on a Unitree G1 humanoid both in simulation and on real hardware, tackling two-handed box transport and one-handed bucket carrying tasks. The robot successfully placed objects at target locations well beyond the reference training range and autonomously recovered from failed grasps, proving that it can reliably complete long-horizon tasks on real hardware.
contributions: Proposed KINO, a hierarchical framework that connects high-level VLM semantic task planning with low-level RL whole-body control using motion keyframes as an intermediate representation.
Developed a saliency-based keyframe sampling strategy that extracts critical motion phases based on body and object acceleration profiles for policy training.
Constructed an inverse kinematics-based retargeting method that adapts library keyframes to the poses and dimensions of real-world objects.
Demonstrated spatial generalization far beyond reference data and autonomous failure recovery on one-handed and two-handed loco-manipulation tasks using a real Unitree G1 humanoid and simulation.

sections.heading: How can we translate language commands into humanoid whole-body motion?
sections.summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation demands both high-level semantic understanding and low-level dynamic balance control. This section explains the motivation and contributions of using compact keyframes as an intermediate interface to bridge the input format gap between VLMs and RL policies.
sections.details:
Loco-manipulation with humanoid robots is a difficult research challenge because the robot must interact with diverse real-world objects across varied environments. When humans perform complex tasks, we seamlessly combine high-level cognitive reasoning with fast, unconscious motor control. Robotics naturally benefits from a similar split into two complementary layers: high-level task planning and low-level motor execution.

Modern VLMs excel at language comprehension and contextual reasoning, and recent VLA models attempt to map visual observations directly to joint motor commands. However, whole-body humanoid control requires delicate contact handling and split-second balance adjustments. Learning this end-to-end via VLAs requires enormous amounts of robot-specific real-world data, which is prohibitively expensive. Meanwhile, reinforcement learning (RL) can learn agile locomotion and object handling by imitating human motion capture data, but stringing multiple skills together for long-horizon tasks end-to-end remains difficult.

The primary barrier to combining them is an interface mismatch. VLMs process abstract, semantic inputs like text and images, whereas RL controllers require precise numerical state observations and structured target goals. To solve this, the authors introduce KINO, a framework using keyframes (whole-body target poses) as an intermediate interface. The VLM focuses strictly on picking the next keyframe from a library, while the RL policy focuses on driving the body to that pose. This division delivers accurate, long-horizon task execution without requiring vast quantities of robot-specific demonstration data.

sections.heading: Where whole-body motion imitation meets foundation model planning
sections.summary: This section reviews prior research in humanoid whole-body control and foundation-model-based robot planning. It highlights the advantages of a sparse keyframe hierarchy over dense reference trajectories and direct end-to-end action outputs.
sections.details:
Related work in this domain spans three key areas:

- Humanoid loco-manipulation: Deep RL has driven major progress in agile locomotion for quadrupeds and humanoids. Methods based on DeepMimic leverage human skeletal similarities to imitate motion capture data. Recent frameworks like HDMI learn manipulation from video, while OmniRetarget retargets human motions while preserving interaction contacts. However, most of these imitation techniques require a dense reference trajectory at inference time, making it hard to adapt flexibly to novel object layouts or field conditions.
- Foundation models for robot planning and control: VLA models that output joint actions directly from images and prompts have mainly been applied to tabletop manipulators and wheeled mobile robots. Applying them to humanoids remains difficult due to the high dimensions and high-frequency balance control required. As a result, using VLMs as high-level reasoning modules rather than direct controllers is a promising direction. In manipulation, methods like ReKep handle relational keypoint constraints, but they do not address dynamic humanoid whole-body control.
- Using motion keyframes: Keyframes have long served as sparse constraints in animation, and robotics frameworks like RobotKeyframing use RL to transition between target poses. However, previous systems relied on humans to provide keyframes manually at run time. KINO integrates these ideas into a fully autonomous system where a VLM automatically selects and commands keyframes based on the evolving scene context.

sections.heading: Inside KINO: Keyframe selection, retargeting, and whole-body control
sections.summary: The framework combines three core elements: a high-level VLM planner, a scene-adaptive retargeting module, and a low-level RL whole-body policy. A crucial innovation is saliency sampling, which uses acceleration profiles to extract meaningful keyframes for policy training.
sections.details:
### III-A Keyframe-conditioned whole-body policy
The low-level controller is an RL policy that receives a target keyframe $\mathcal{K}_t$ and outputs joint-level actions (PD target angles $\boldsymbol{a}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{29}$). Observations include base velocities, the gravity vector, joint positions and velocities, action history, the object's local pose, and the target keyframe $\mathcal{K}_t = (\boldsymbol{\hat{p}}^r_t, \boldsymbol{\hat{R}}^r_t, \boldsymbol{\hat{q}}_t, \boldsymbol{\hat{p}}^o_t, \boldsymbol{\hat{Q}}^o_t)$. The policy is trained with PPO in an asymmetric Actor-Critic setup, where privileged data (such as reference trajectories and tracking errors) is provided only to the Critic. Rewards are divided into reference tracking, goal reaching, and regularization terms, trained via a multi-critic architecture to prevent conflicting objective gradients.

### III-B Robot keyframes and saliency sampling
Keyframes provided by the VLM at inference time are very sparse. If the policy is trained by uniformly sampling keyframes from reference motions, the training distribution ends up dominated by unremarkable mid-stride locomotion frames. Crucial events like picking up or setting down an object are rarely sampled. To fix this, the authors identify local maxima in the whole-body composite acceleration profile $\Gamma(t) = \sum_j \|\ddot{\mathbf{p}}_j(t)\|_2$ to find moments of rapid kinematic change. They filter out periodic leg acceleration peaks caused by walking cycles, keeping the frames synchronized with peaks in vertical object acceleration. This saliency-based sampling ensures the low-level policy focuses heavily on the decisive milestone poses that dictate task success.

### III-C Scene alignment: Retargeting and path planning
Because library keyframes are built for standard object dimensions, they must be adjusted for actual objects in the scene. First, the robot's end-effectors and torso horizontal positions are adjusted via similarity transformations based on the detected object pose. Next, a damped least-squares inverse kinematics (IK) solver updates joint angles, applying heavy weights to vertical foot residuals to keep both feet firmly on the ground. For locomotion, the system plans curvature-constrained Dubins paths to generate smooth intermediate keyframe sequences, respecting the turn-rate limits present in the training motions.

### III-D VLM-based planner
The high-level VLM planner (based on open models such as Qwen2.5-VL-72B) takes task instructions, top-down camera images, and robot execution feedback (success flags and error metrics from the previous step) as its prompt. It outputs structured JSON specifying the next keyframe name, an object interaction flag, and a task completion flag. This runs as an event-driven closed loop: the planner queries the VLM once the robot stops and completes its prior sub-task. If a sub-task fails, the VLM autonomously re-issues the keyframe to initiate a recovery attempt.

sections.heading: Sim and real-world results: High precision from sparse commands and broad generalization
sections.summary: Evaluations in simulation and on a Unitree G1 humanoid tested one-handed and two-handed transport tasks. The proposed saliency sampling boosted overall task success from 44% to 92%, and the robot achieved broad spatial generalization and autonomous recovery.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulation evaluation and spatial generalization
In simulation, the framework was tested on two-handed box transport and one-handed bucket carrying. VLM inference took under 0.2 seconds on average, and retargeting required roughly 5 milliseconds. The system demonstrated impressive spatial generalization. Although the reference training motions only covered a confined rectangular area near the origin, KINO's combination of intermediate path planning and keyframe control enabled over 90% success rates when placing boxes at distant locations (over 4 meters forward or off to the sides), far beyond the training distribution.

### IV-B Real humanoid deployment
Experiments were conducted on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid using internal proprioception coupled with an external motion capture system for object tracking. The VLM selected keyframes from the appropriate motion library (two-handed box carrying or one-handed bucket carrying) based on user instructions. The physical robot completed picking, transporting, and placing sequences reliably without tipping over.

### IV-C Keyframe sampling ablation
To evaluate the saliency-based sampling method, the authors compared it against a baseline policy trained with uniform 1.5-second time-interval sampling. Over 100 evaluation trials, the uniform sampling policy achieved only a 44% overall task success rate, while the proposed method reached 92%. A detailed breakdown showed that both approaches achieved 97–99% success during the approach phase, but uniform sampling failed frequently during contact-critical pick and place phases. Focusing policy training on key transition points proved vital for overall performance.

### IV-D Failure detection and recovery
Because the VLM planner continuously monitors error metrics and visual context, it handles physical slip-ups gracefully. For example, if the robot's hands miss the box during a grasp attempt, the VLM recognizes the failure, commands the robot to stand back up, and re-triggers the approach and crouch keyframes to retry the pick autonomously.

sections.heading: Takeaways and next steps: The path to full real-world autonomy
sections.summary: This section summarizes KINO's success in connecting VLMs to whole-body RL controllers via keyframes. It also reviews current limitations, such as manual library construction and reliance on motion capture, pointing toward future fully onboard RGB-D setups.
sections.details:
This work introduced KINO, a hierarchical framework for long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation. By using motion keyframes as an intermediate interface between a high-level VLM and an RL whole-body controller, the system combines flexible semantic reasoning with robust dynamic control without needing massive robot-specific demonstrations. Saliency-based sampling raised end-to-end success rates from 44% to 92%, and the system demonstrated strong zero-shot spatial generalization and autonomous recovery from grasp errors.

Nevertheless, several limitations remain. First, the keyframe library and natural language annotations were constructed manually. Future efforts should automate keyframe discovery and semantic labeling using VLMs to scale up library creation. Second, the current setup relies on external motion capture for object pose tracking and an overhead camera for VLM visual input. Transitioning to onboard RGB-D cameras and head-mounted vision is the essential next step toward achieving fully untethered autonomy in unconstrained real-world environments.

takeaways: Restricting the VLM to picking representative intermediate keyframes instead of issuing raw motor actions is highly effective, improving both sample efficiency and balance robustness for humanoids.

When training policies to follow keyframes, sampling based on physical saliency (such as acceleration peaks) rather than uniform time intervals dramatically improves performance during contact-heavy phases, raising success rates from 44% to 92%.
Geometrically retargeting library keyframes enables zero-shot spatial generalization to novel object sizes and locations far outside the original reference motion data.
limitations: Building the initial keyframe library and annotating it with natural language requires manual effort, limiting scalability across diverse tasks.
Object pose estimation in real-world experiments relies on an external motion capture system rather than purely onboard sensors.
The VLM planner uses images from a fixed third-person overhead camera, meaning closed-loop execution using solely egocentric, onboard cameras remains future work.
